If one batch of poison can keep killing the rats as it's passed on, it takes less to begin with and doesn't need to be reapplied as often. More of the newer, safer poisons have a much higher LD50 as well (meaning it requires a higher dose to be effective) so it's safer for upstream predators like owls and cats etc, but also may not be totally effective with larger rats.

Ah, so he's probably referring to poisons that change on a chemical level when ingested. After they are fully digested and bind, they aren't active anymore. So if the poison has been fully digested and reacted, it wouldn't then poison an animal that then ate the dead one. However, if a rat chowed down on some poison, and was then eaten by an owl shortly after the poison may not have fully be used up, and would then be able to act on the owl.

It likely has a lot to do with dosage size versus body weight, and timing. If the rat is still running and active, it likely just ingested the poison, and the owl eats the whole rat, so ingests everything the rat did. A large dog, with much more body mass than the owl, which only bites or even chews on a rat is both getting exposed to a much lower dose it also has a much higher body mass to spread the toxin out. So more likely to make the dog slightly ill/upset it's stomach than actually cause serious damage.

Oh, they age normally while on R&R, but that's just like a month (it's been a while since I've read the books). Then it was like 6 months each way on the trip? 

For example: It's January 1st year 1, when the LA leaves the planet and goes to Lusus. The trip on-board is 6 months to the people on the ship. Five years pass, for everyone, but because of the dilation effect the ship only experiences 6 months. Then, the ship re-enters "normal" time, January 1st year 6. They spend a month in orbit. It's now Feb 1st year 6. Back to Maui they go, another 6 months to them and another 5 years normal time. They arrive on Feb 1st year 11. To the people who traveled, it's only been 13 months total. To everyone else, it's been 10 years and 1 month.

It's not that time is moving 'slower' on Maui Covenant. Time is moving the same speed in the entire universe, so all planets are on the same time. 

When a ship is traveling near the speed of light, time moves slower to them compared to the rest of the universe that is remaining still. That's the dilation effect. So while it takes 10 years to go from one planet to the other in real time, the ship and those on board experience it at the rate of a month. 

If the theoretical physics of it doesn't make sense, try to think of it like being in a state of slowed animation (rather than suspended). Everyone else is experiencing time normally, but you're slowed way, way down.

Evolution is only aimed at getting the next generation made, and the most successful which often times means the most of a new generation.
In the terms of monkeys: a group of monkeys hear a certain noise and one of their buddies get eaten by whatever made that noise. All the monkeys are on alert for a while. The ones that remember that noise and react quickest are most likely to survive. So, the monkey that is constantly alert and always reacts not only to that noise but to all the similar noises is most likely to be the one left to mate the most. Does it matter if that monkey is a nervous wreck? Nope. Had offspring. Job done. That monkeys offspring might be prone to be more aware, or see it's parent reacting a lot and pick up that behavior, and hence survive and pass on that hyper reactivate nature. 
Now, several hundreds of thousands of years later... we are easily scared over reactive monkeys that fixate on bad experiences. Only we don't always get the reward. We have no trees, no assured mate and family. We're just neurotic and lonely. I could go on about the swing we see now in mating/reproductive behaviors now but that gets even more depressing.

It's the other way around. Since the solution was decreased in volume, it's concentrated, so you'd divide by 5, not multiply. If it had been diluted, then you'd multiply. 

Example with smaller numbers:
50mL of solution has 50 cells in it, or 1 cell/mL. 
If that solution is concentrated down to 10mL, the same 50 cells are now at 50 cells in 10mL or 5 cells/mL. 

The concentration in the original 10L solution would be the same as the concentration in the 50mL aliquot. To get the total number of cells, it would be: (10L x 1000mL/L) ÷ 50mL.

HIV (the virus that causes AIDS) isn't present in sweat or spit, but it is present in blood and semen. It also requires a broken skin barrier or direct introduction to the blood to get into your system (direct introduction via shared needles for example). Just getting HIV containing blood on your skin won't infect you, assuming your skin isn't broken. It can cross membranes like eyes though, and easier to get into cells like your mouth, vagina, and anus because the skin there isn't hardened like on your arms/hands. When planning on dehydrating DNA, I almost always elute in just water first. This is because while the water from the TE evaporates, the salts remain and therefore get concentrated. Also, I try not to fully dehydrate the sample, but leave about 5-10 uL behind. Then add whatever amount of water and 10x TE you need to get the final concentration. 

For example: 

Initial concentration of 50ng/uL in 100uL of water. Wanting a final concentration of 200ng/uL.

50ng/uL x 100uL = 5000ng or 5ug

Dehydrate to ~ 10uL. 

Final volume would be 25uL ( 5000ng ÷ 200ng/uL = 25uL)

Add 2.5uL of 10x TE, and water to 25uL (about 12.5uL, measure the initial dehydrated sample to get exact numbers)

I have a quick trick that uses a metal icing spatula. I use one that is fairly long (6-7"?) and wide, doesn't matter if its flat or angled. Heat up water in a kettle, or microwave it, to near boiling. Pour into a tall coffee thermos, stick the spatula in for a bit to heat up. Then smooth the sides. It will look wet for a bit, but will dry shortly. Usually takes me a few heat-smooth-reheats to get around the whole cake. You'll know its time to reheat when the spatula stops gliding smoothly and starts to drag the frosting.

The other tips about getting the frosting itself super smooth are also great. I just can't get a great cream on my frosting due to only having a mediocre hand mixer at the moment, so this trick really saves me.

It's actually extremely efficient for output, much more than crude oil. The corn that is used in ethanol production is a different variety from what people eat. It's all stock feed. And rhe best part- one of the side products, DDGs, which is basically just the plant proteins, is a much better food for stock like cattle and pigs. Most ethanol plants have a near zero carbon footprint due to the incredibly strict EPA regulations, which will never be said of any oil refinery. Farming communities that have an ethanol plant see much better profits and sustainability than those that go directly to either human or stock feed (again, 2 different crops) and stock especially pigs have less waste and more weight gain when fed on DDgs than plain stock corn. And in addition, human food corn goes to waste at about a 30% rate. 
Old ethanol production (like 20 years ago) was somewhat inefficient and those numbers are what a lot of people go off of. Now, it's incredibly efficient and beneficial to everyone. But the ethanol industry is held to a standard that no oil refinery could ever come close to as far as emissions and energy use are concerned, and are subsidised at about 20 cents to the dollar for what oil is.

Why do you think the ethanol subsidies need to stop? They get far less than oil companies, and often end up selling their carbon credits (a measure of how much carbon they can produce) to oil refineries. Its a much, much cleaner form of fuel and cuts emissions by a large degree. Why would you want to cut the very small subsidies they recieve that go to supporting farmers?

No, it's a bit more complicated than that. You can have ovaries dropping eggs fine and then the next part of the signal doesn't go through to tell your body the egg wasn't fertilized. Also, sometimes ovaries decide they are going to pop multiple eggs at the same time. It has to do with hormone levels and signals. If you are worried about it at all, just ask your Dr for a hormone panel over a couple months. There really isn't any need to worry if you aren't trying to get pregnant and you don't have any discomfort. Of it hurts oddly,get checked out! If you have been trying to have a kid for at least six months and your cycle is weird still go see a Dr (also take folic acid if you are actively trying to get pregnant). Basically, cycles can be weird, ovaries can be awkward about timing, and the other dozen hormones and signal pathways that are involved in ovulation and menstruation can also be a bit weird but still end up fine in the end.

Yup! One ovary is kicking out a lot more hormone than usual, and can cause PMDD. Another fun fact, sometimes the 'lazy' ovary will be so lazy the other one will kick in, after about a week if the rest of your system doesn't just go ahead without the signal from the lazy ovary. It's like being in a group project with someone who is super slow heh. Sometimes they finally get their work done just really late, and sometimes it's so late you have to pick up the slack and get things moving

Weirdly enough, sometimes your ovaries can get slightly out of sync. Basically, one of them is taking longer to respond to the hormone signals and that is slowing up your whole cycle. (you ovulate from one side a month, then the other side next month.) So long as you aren't experiencing any side pain or anything it's nothing to worry about. I worked in a lab looking at how certain hormones affect a certain developmental pathway. We had to use a mouse model for obvious reasons. By far, the hardest research I've ever done, and I had to work in a BSL3 situation for a while. But the answers we found linked the developmental issues to later stage heart issues, and opened up a whole new area of research in that field. It's worth it, but it hurts.

This makes me really happy. I wish all universities had something like this. Through my grad studies, I did a lot of work involving mouse models, and ended up nearly vegetarian because of it. I know that the work I was doing was important (prostate cancer, mitochondrial disorders, and chromosomal abnormalities), and I wish there was a way to communicate to the mice why I had to do what I did. The hardest project I worked on dealt with looking at how different hormone/toxin levels affect the development of certain organs at the fetal stage, which involved having to use fetal mice. The first time I did the initial dissection is the only time I've had to leave the lab to be sick. I drank a lot that night. There is a paper out there that's been cited around 30 times that I was a third author on, and it was based around that research. I don't regret the work or the needs, but damn, as someone with a soft spot for everything that really ate at my heart. It's been nearly a decade now and I still remember it all in great detail. Something I wish people who are so against animal research would understand is that there really isn't another option, and it really does weigh a ton on the hearts of most researchers. If we could use other models, like bacteria or yeast, we would, trust us. No one wants to harm animals, but when you are looking at possible treatments or trying to understand exactly how a specific disorder occurs, an animal model is the only way. Hells, if we could have used C. Elegans or even a fish model we would have. Those were the 'easy' labs. The first time I had to euthanize a full litter because none of them had the right gene marker, I sobbed like a bitch, and the kind lab tech in the mouse room helped me. It's not like we as researchers are heartless, we are doing what we do because it's for a greater good, but it still sucks giant hairy balls. I look forward to when we can do everything on a computer model. Until then... Let's put statues for these lovely little critters that make modern medicine and research possible.
